newsitem.title: COMOROS: Hijacked Ethiopian plane crashes, 50 survive.
newsitem.headline: Hijacked Ethiopian plane crashes, 50 survive.

text.p: At least 50 people were killed when a hijacked Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 with 175 passengers and crew aboard crashed into the sea near the Comoro Islands after running out of fuel.

Ethiopian Airlines in Addis Ababa said that 50 survivors had so far been found since the plane came down on Saturday in the Indian Ocean off East Africa and the director of a local radio station said the whole island had been mobilised in the search for survivors and bodies.
"There are about 50 injured according to the latest news. The majority don't have serious injuries, less than 10 are seriously injured," Mohamed Cheikh of Radio des Iles told Reuters.
Ahmed Chanfe, deputy manager at the Comoros' main airport, said in a telephone interview that 50 bodies had been recovered.

The plane, flight ET 961, was hijacked on Saturday morning soon after it took off from Addis Ababa before its first scheduled stop in the Kenyan capital Nairobi en route to Abidjan via Brazzaville and Lagos.

Airline officials said the hijackers were believed to be transit passengers from Bombay. They said the identity of the hijackers was not confirmed but that they may have wanted to hijack the plane to Australia.
Airline officials said the pilot and one crew member were among those who survived when the plane ran out of fuel and ditched while trying to land at Moroni airport.

Thirty bodies of crash victims, mostly Asians and Africans, were laid out under blankets in the conference room of a beach hotel near where the plane came down about 25 km (16 miles) north of the airport outside the capital of the Indian Ocean archipelago.
Ethiopian Airlines said it would issue a passenger list on Sunday but aviation officials in Nairobi said that at least 25 non-Africans were aboard.

The aviation sources in Nairobi said seven Britons, four French, three Italians, two Americans, eight Israelis and a Hungarian were among the passengers on the plane. The British foreign office said it believed eight Britons were aboard.

Diplomats in Addis Ababa identified the Hungarian as Hungary's ambassador to Ethiopia and Kenya while the Italian news agency ANSA said the Italian passengers included two employees at the Italian embassy in Addis Ababa.

Comoro state radio appealed to all doctors to report to the two main hospitals on Grande Comore, the island where Moroni is situated. Tourists at the hotel, reportedly including a group of 20 French doctors on holiday, rushed to join the rescue effort.
Speaking earlier to the BBC World Service, Frederick Chretien, manager of the Hotel Le Galawa, said a survivor spoke of seeing two hijackers on board.
Chretien said there was little information about the demands of the hijackers. But he said one of the survivors he had spoken to said the men were panicky.

"He said there were two (men) quite panicky and trying to get in contact with the Ethiopian government and they couldn't get through and that's why they started to turn in the middle of the Indian Ocean until there was no fuel."
Airline officials said the plane was carrying 163 passengers and 12 crew members.
Witnesses said the plane broke in two when it plunged into the sea.
"The plane skimmed the ground, went over the Galawa hotel ... made a big noise and crashed," one witness told Reuters.
"We saw the aircraft going down and down and down towards the hotel just in front of the main beach and then fall into the water... The aircraft is broken into two pieces," Chretien said.
Airline officials said the fuselage was seen floating in the sea while the rear part had submerged.
"The plane crashed at around 3:20 local time (1220 GMT)," Chakira Maamoune, a Moroni airport official, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Airline officials in the Tanzanian capital Dar es Salaam said they made contact with the plane at about 3 p.m. (1200 GMT). Tanzania is on the east coast of Africa bordering the Indian Ocean.
"The control tower had some contact with the plane but only for five minutes, then it was cut. At that point the plane was around the coastal area of Dar es Salaam," the official said.
Ethiopian Airlines is the only airline that crosses the breadth of Africa and has had one of the best safety records among African carriers.
